edits.walkthrough_append: Worked check: test the ideal against one breach — a Brahmana reduced to farming, or a shudra ruling as a king (as the texts admit happened): the theory calls such cases varna-samkara, mixture, and explains them away; the evidence calls them normal history. Empires were run by ministers of low birth; provinces by kings of mixed descent. For the board examination, questions on the varna order's limits are answered with the ideal restated in one line, then two documented breaches, and the closing argument that prescriptive texts reveal anxieties precisely where practice diverged from prescription.

Worked check: read one rule historically — the Dharmasutra rule that a shudra may not hear the Veda, and the Manusmriti's punishments scaled by varna for the same offence: the escalating penalties map the hierarchy's logic better than any abstract statement. Note the genre difference too: sutras in terse prose, shastras in verse with commentary. For the board examination, normative-text answers give the two genres with dates, name three subjects they regulate (marriage, inheritance, punishments), and close with the source-criticism line that these are prescriptions of a learned elite, evidence of ideals and anxieties, not transcripts of practice.

Worked check: read the same rulers through three mirrors — the Brahmanical texts call the Nandas of low birth and the Mauryas questionable in pedigree; Buddhist and Jaina traditions honour Chandragupta's connection to their teachers; Greek accounts (Megasthenes, Justin) describe a powerful dynast without any pedigree anxiety. The difference lies in who wrote, and for whom. For the board examination, questions on conflicting representations expect the three sources with their verdicts, and the closing historiographical line: accusations of low origin are a Brahmanical genre of political disparagement, not a census record.

Worked check: test the theory against one real group — the Manusmriti derives castes like the Suta (bard-charioteer) from a Brahmana mother and Kshatriya father, explaining a living profession by a hypothetical marriage; the reality is that occupational groups existed whether or not the taxonomy had a slot for them. Varna-samkara is thus a theory of anomalies, not a record of marriages. For the board examination, questions on intermixture expect the definition, one named mixed caste with its textual parentage, and the critical reading: the very elaborateness of the scheme shows how hard reality pressed on the four-fold frame.

Worked check: meet the outside groups in the texts' own words — forest peoples (atavika, nishada), the mountain and desert communities, nomadic pastoralists — described by settled society as wild, pre-Aryan or demonic, yet courted by kings for elephants, hired as guides, and converted by Buddhist missionaries. Beyond the frame did not mean beyond the state's reach or the market's. For the board examination, questions on groups outside varna expect the terms with meanings, their economic roles, and the closing argument that the varna model was a map of the settled plain, not of the subcontinent — the outside was part of the world.

Worked check: read the Gita's redefinition against the Dharmasutra's — where the sutras fix varna by birth, the Gita's four varnas are fixed by the qualities (guna) and actions (karma) of nature: teaching, protecting, producing, serving as qualities apportioned among all. Yet Krishna also binds Arjuna to his own swadharma — the warrior's duty — so birth-duty survives inside the new frame. For the board examination, Gita questions expect this double reading: the qualitative recast and the practical retention of duty, ending that the text universalises the order while commanding obedience to it — theology stabilising hierarchy.

Worked check: scale the vows to their audiences — the five Mahavratas bind the monk absolutely: not to injure, lie, steal, be unchaste, or possess; the laity take the five Anuvratas, the little vows, softened to suit household life — truthfulness, limited possessions, no unnecessary violence. The two-tier design is how a demanding ethic became a community. For the board examination, Jain-vows answers list the five with translations, state the monk-lay contrast with one example (possession: renunciation versus honest livelihood), and close that the graded ethic let Jainism survive as both monastery and merchant community.

Worked check: trace the split to its practices — under a famine, part of the community migrated south under Bhadrabahu while the rest stayed; on reunion, the stayers had adopted white robes and adjusted the vows; the returners held to complete nudity and the original discipline. From disputes over dress, discipline and the canon grew the Digambara and Shvetambara orders, each with its own image of the tirthankaras. For the board examination, sect questions give the famine narrative with its clear historical caveat, the three points of difference (dress, mahavratas, liberation of women), and the consequence: separate canons and traditions.

Worked check: read the four sights as the biography's hinge — the sheltered prince rides out and meets in one day an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a serene ascetic; the first three name the problem, the fourth its possible answer; the great departure follows. Historians read the palace seclusion as narrative art and the renunciation as historical act. For the board examination, Buddha-life questions expect the birth and clan (Sakya of Kapilavastu), the four sights in order, the renunciation, enlightenment at Bodh Gaya and first sermon at Sarnath — biography told as a dated, place-anchored sequence.

Worked check: state the truths as a diagnosis — suffering exists (birth, age, illness, death, union with the unloved); suffering has a cause, thirst or craving; craving can be ended; the ending lies on the eightfold path of right view through right meditation. Medical metaphor by design: symptom, cause, prognosis, prescription. For the board examination, Four-Noble-Truths answers list the four in order with the Pali term arya satya, unpack craving as the hinge, and close that the path is neither ritual nor speculation but training — which is why the Buddha called his teaching a raft, to be used, not worshipped.

Worked check: read the sangha as an institution, not just an ideal — admission by ordination before ten elders; the fortnightly patimokkha recitation where faults are confessed; the vassa retreat binding monks to place; disputes settled by procedures in the Vinaya. Women were admitted later, with eight additional rules, an organisation the texts record without hiding. For the board examination, sangha answers define the order, name the Vinaya and patimokkha, describe two procedures showing self-governance, and close with the social significance: men and women, all varnas, admitted — the most open door in early India.

Worked check: date and place the four councils — Rajagriha shortly after the Buddha's death (first recitation by Ananda and Upali), Vaishali a century later (where the second schism brewed over monastic rules), Pataliputra under Ashoka (the Abhidhamma recitation, per southern tradition), and Kanauj under Kanishka (commentary composition, per northern tradition). Each council is a snapshot of the canon at that date, and each is followed by a division. For the board examination, council answers give patron, place and outcome for all four, and close that the councils' history is the history of the canon's growth and the sects' birth.

Worked check: read a stupa anatomically — the anda (dome) on a rounded base, relic casket buried in the core, the harmika railing-crown atop, the yasthi and chhatra above it, the pradakshina path and vedika railings around, four torana gateways at the cardinal points (Sanchi's the finest). Every part carries meaning: circumambulation clockwise, relic at the axis, dome as firmament. For the board examination, stupa answers label the parts on a sketch, give Asoka's relic-distribution as the historical start, and close with donative inscriptions — kings, guilds, monks and nuns paying for rails and gateways — the society recorded on its own monument.

Worked check: follow one sutta into three languages — the Buddha taught in the people's Prakrit; the Pali canon (Tipitaka: Vinaya, Sutta, Abhidhamma) preserves the Theravada recension; northern traditions translated into Sanskrit and Central Asian tongues, adding sutras the south never knew (the Lotus, the Pure Land texts). Same teacher, different linguistic canons. For the board examination, textual-tradition answers name the three baskets in one line each, the Pali versus Sanskrit division with the schools behind them, and close that language history and sect history are the same history in Buddhism.

Worked check: read the Kitab-ul-Hind's architecture — six sections (the Fraser order: on religion and philosophy, then sciences, social order, geography, history, astronomy), written in Arabic, structured as question and answer so the reader must judge each claim against the next; Al-Biruni learned Sanskrit to read the sources themselves, and says so. Method before opinion. For the board examination, Al-Biruni answers give his origin, the year of his arrival with Mahmud's circle, the book's languages and structure, and his own declared method — weighing Sanskrit texts against observation — which is why historians rank him the first Indologist.

Worked check: compare two theories of caste across the book — Al-Biruni reports the Brahmanical four-varna doctrine with its scriptural sanctions, then offers his own comparison: castes as a social institution like the classes and guilds of the ancient Iranians, a human arrangement, not divine order — a strikingly secular aside for his century. He notes untouchability's miseries without endorsing it. For the board examination, caste-analysis questions expect the four-varna summary as he gives it, the comparison-with-antiquity method, and the closing observation that an outsider's eye saw social construction where insiders saw sacred order.

Worked check: follow one critique to its reason — Al-Biruni praises Indian achievements in mathematics (the numerals, the zero) and astronomy's inheritance from the Greeks, then asks why the sciences have stagnated: his answer is isolation — India is ringed by mountains and seas, its scholars write in Sanskrit for themselves, contemptuous of foreign learning, and bound by taboos that fence inquiry. Criticism from admiration, not contempt. For the board examination, his critique is answered with the three charges (isolation, language barrier, taboo-bound thinking), one field where he credits India (mathematics), and the closing note that he wrote as a scientist comparing systems, not as a polemicist.

Worked check: read the Rihla as layers — what Ibn Battuta saw (the bazaars, the postal riders, the punishment at the Sultan's court), what he felt (his awe, his quarrels, his fear of falling from favour), and what the qazi-lawyer habit made him notice (procedures, offices, appointments). The book is travelogue, memoir and office-log in one. For the board examination, questions on Ibn Battuta expect the biography (Morocco, thirty years on the road, qazi in Delhi), the book written at the Sultan of Morocco's command, and the dual value: texture of daily life plus eyewitness court history.

Worked check: weigh his Delhi as a witness weighs it — he marvels at the city's size, the palace's maqsub domes and the hundred-pillared hall; he lists the gifts and posts he received; and he also reports the Sultan's severity: the carved hands at the gate, the daily executions, his own fear. admiration and dread sit in the same chapter. For the board examination, Delhi-observation answers give the city and palace description, the Sultan's patronage as Ibn Battuta experienced it, the cruelty documented without euphemism, and the closing judgement that this double view makes him a source both for urban grandeur and for the despotism that funded it.

Worked check: follow one commodity chain through his eyes — the coconut: he describes the tree's every use, from the drink in the nut to the thatch above the roof and the rope that stitches Malabar's ships; the bazaars he prices by quarter (the grain market, the slave market, the horse market, for horses could not breed in India and were imported at fortune's price). For the board examination, town-and-economy answers give the bazaar description with its quarters, the coconut or areca example fully worked, and the closing point that his commercial detail — prices, imports, trades — is what makes the Rihla economic history too.

Worked check: clock the system he measured — the dawa posts stood at fixed intervals with relay runners, and the uluq horse posts at four-mile stages with remounts standing ready; a letter from Delhi to the distant provinces travelled, Ibn Battuta says, at speeds no ordinary courier could match — the Sultan's intelligence and the state's orders moved on it. For the board examination, postal-system answers name both tiers with their runners-and-stations mechanics, the speed claim as he reports it, and the closing interpretation: the post was the Sultanate's nervous system — intelligence, orders and grain-price reports — the infrastructure of control.

Worked check: map the movement's novelty — sixty-three Nayanars and twelve Alvars, from priest to potter to woman-saint, sang in Tamil the god they loved, and their hymns were collected under later royal patronage (the Shaiva canon by Nambi Andar Nambi under the Cholas); the temples those hymns named became the sacred geography of the south. Devotion made caste-crossing saints before any doctrine argued for it. For the board examination, Nayanar-Alvar answers give the counts, the period, the languages and deities, the social range with one named low-caste saint, and the closing point that the hymns built south India's temple world.

Worked check: read one hymn as history — Appar's verses on service to the shrine, Sambandar's on the god of the dancing hall, Sundarar's familiar complaints that treat Shiva as a friend who owes him gifts: three voices, one god, and through them a temple-centred religion taking shape in Tamil, not Sanskrit. For the board examination, Nayanar answers name the trio, give one line of flavour for each (service, doctrine, intimacy), the Chola canonisation of the hymns, and the closing argument that vernacular devotion gave Shaivism its mass base centuries before Sanskrit philosophy did.

Worked check: read Kabir's method — he sneers at both temples and mosques ('the stone is deaf'), riddles the divine into ordinary things (the drop in the ocean, the weaving of cloth), and speaks in the weaver's idiom of the sant-bhasha, which is why his verses passed into the Granth Sahib and the Panch Vani alike. Legend makes him born Muslim and raised by a weaver, disciples of both communities claimed him, and both claimed his body at death. For the board examination, Kabir answers give the nirguna definition, the attack on hollow ritual, one verse image quoted, and the legacy: a poet claimed by every community precisely because he belonged to none.

Worked check: place the Nath yogis in bhakti's landscape — Gorakhnath's order taught hatha yoga, treasured the body as the instrument of liberation, roamed in the clothes of the dead; Kabir's poems scold them for arrogance even while borrowing their idiom of the inner journey; alchemy and healing drew householders to them. The tradition stood beside bhakti, sometimes rival, sometimes tributary. For the board examination, Nath-tradition answers define the panth and its founder-legend, name two practices (hatha yoga, alchemy), and close with the interaction argument: nirguna saints attacked the yogis' pride while absorbing their vocabulary — the religions of medieval India grew by argument.
